rv.q: “Be More Chill” is one of the strongest new musicals of the past decade, a charming, astutely crafted tale of neurotic post-millennial geeks in love whose appeal is in no way limited to those whom it portrays.

As bouncy and silly and fanciful as Be More Chill can get, it rarely talks down to its audiences, and a show that accomplishes that, and does it so well, deserves ever new audiences, perhaps even those more familiar with plush Broadway seats.
The zippy, delightfully devilish Be More Chill
The internet sensation gets a Broadway upgrade that gives it more universal appeal.

"There is a breathless quality to everything that squeaky baritone Roland does in his attempt to break free and be cool. And those thrills aren’t just for kids. Traditional theatergoing audiences...will find delicious favor in Iconis’ contagious melodies and tricky lyrics...

For one thing, it is — by cold critical standards — the worst of the lot, with a repetitive score, painfully forced rhymes, cartoonish acting and a general approach that mistakes decibel level (literally and metaphorically) for emotional intensity.
And, perhaps weirdest of all, it always feels like you’re watching a cast that is l-o-n-g past high-school, all playing, like, sophomores.
But however much you root for it, Be More Chill ultimately seems like a talented, likable team that is playing in the wrong league, and the Lyceum looms around it like a judgment.
Exhaustingly exaggerated, the show should consider an advisory that some material might not be suitable for adults.
For my part, I find the implicit messages the material sends to young people repellent enough that I would advocate for impressionable minds to take in this musical with caution.

“Be More Shrill” would be a better title for director Stephen Brackett’s heinously overamplified and overacted production, built on the story of a nerd played by the intrepid Will Roland, who takes a magic pill to become popular with the high school “in” crowd.
Its combination of humor, social commentary, catchy music, and spectacular staging is everything a Broadway musical should be.

In the words of Be More Chill, this show is “lit AF,” so get your tickets while you still can and be a part of the Broadway premiere of what is surely destined to become a 21st-century classic and to number among the all-time favorite musicals of the Great White Way.
By the time Jeremy belts out his final number, “Voices in My Head," you'll be hearing those voices, too, in a wow of a musical that comes on like gangbusters.

"Iconis’ tunes, which have earned him a major online following, are character-driven and catchy...But a lot of Iconis’ songs, and Vizzini’s story, gets lost in the chaos at the Lyceum. Director Stephen Brackett isn’t much for subtlety or soft moments. Roland, ideally cast in so many ways, is pushing too hard—vocally and otherwise...
If one’s hearing may be jeopardized, this production is well worth seeing.
If you want to check out what the musical theater kids are excited about, Be More Chill will do nicely.

"A sublimely silly, exciting sci-fi teen musical comedy...A pop-rock score by Joe Iconis that is both addictively catchy and a master class in post-Sondheim dramatic integration...It brings fresh air and youthful vitality...The show’s weakest link is Joe Tracz’s book, which occasionally sputters and resorts to pandering...
Now Be More Chill is on Broadway, with an upgrade in production values and the excellent Off

"Blenderizes teen tuner tropes...But Joe Tracz’s book and Joe Iconis’s score provide enough originality and zip to compensate for the familiarity. Stephen Brackett’s direction and Chase Brock’s choreography keep the action moving quickly and smartly enough to gloss over any dull patches...

Joe Iconis, long thought to be one of the most promising new theater composers, makes good on that promise, and Joe Tracz demonstrates for a second time that he can put difficult material on the stage.
The problem is that those stakes still never feel high enough, and the show is the exact opposite of chill throughout.
Its story is most sincere when its teenagers are thinking over the mess of their lives.

Spending two and a half hours with them feels at times like being stuck in detention.
These overwrought people on stage recall the street performers in nearby Times Square.
The show is a high-octane delight, which will have audiences tapping their feet to Joe Iconis's score throughout the show.
Some may find the musical’s frenetic energy and juvenile worldview tiresome.

One of the best things about Tracz’s book and Iconis’ lyrics is that while most of the characters seem one-dimensional at first, they are given more sides, some quite surprising, in the course of the musical’s two acts.

"A sci-fi parable of digital life and teenage insecurity...Sleek and shiny, sardonically teen-focused, duty-bound by the aesthetic eclecticism of today’s youth and built by a score that sounds nearly like a 2008. Vampire Weekend mixtape...
I'm raising my original Show Score from 55 to 70 because I came away even more appreciative of the talented company, each of whom displays exemplary comical, musical, and dancing skills.
It's not for everyone, but it is a distinctive entry in the crowded market of Broadway high school musicals.
It’s not a masterpiece, but I get what its fans see in it.
An inconsistent tone, making a joke of bisexuality, and more are bugs in its system.
Relentlessly hyperactive, broad, and sophomoric, it still lacks the sophistication, polish, and emotional resonance of its high school musical peers, but it is infectiously fun.

This to-thine-own-self-be-true fable is rather messy, presumably intended to be so by writer Tracz: the Playbill program notes express thanks to author Vizzini for “inspiring a generation of messy, beautiful people.”
Few of the songs are memorable. However, 'Michael in the Bathroom' is perhaps the most carefully written and the most sensitively delivered.

Directed by Stephen Brackett, the show is a technicolor, high energy swirl of buzzwords and ideas that a corporate boardroom thought might appeal to Today's Youth but miss the mark.
But Be More Chill is as confused and un-self-aware as a hormonal teenage boy — and nearly as reckless.
The comedy and fun fly brilliantly.

cn.t: Critics are split on this viral sensation's Broadway bow: fans embrace its energetic score and sincere take on teen angst, but detractors find it frenetic, overwrought, and lacking the substance to match its online hype.

sg.ra: Center orchestra rows D-G offer head-on sightlines to the high stage without neck strain. Gentle rake; intimate 922-seat house means even mid-orchestra feels close. Playbill notes Oh, Mary! action is downstage center, rewarding central seats.

Telecharge lists extreme sides of the first 11 orchestra rows as obstructed-view seats per Playbill. SeatPlan confirms double-digit seats are angled with far-side stage obstruction. 1903 house geometry leaves sharp side angles near stage.

sg.n: Orchestra Rear (Rows L-O, behind mezz overhang)
sg.ra: TickPick and SeatPlan both confirm Mezzanine overhang begins at Row L of Orchestra. AVFMS reviewer for O12 praised tiered rake ('raised above the row in front so you don't have any heads blocking you'). Fine for plays; top-of-stage cutoff limits tall-set musicals.

SeatPlan: 'patrons can look directly down to the stage, taking advantage of the Mezzanine's fantastic aerial views which don't sacrifice detail.' Excellent rake prevents blocked views. Ideal for spectacle/musicals where staging composition matters.

Folliesbroadway and Headout both flag Mezz D-F center as best value: clean sightlines, excellent rake, priced materially below front-mezz/prime-orchestra. Balcony overhang doesn't cut in until Row C so D-F also sit past the cutoff line without being affected (SeatPlan note is about row C).

sg.n: Mezzanine Rear (behind Row C — balcony overhang) and Side Double-Digits
sg.ra: SeatPlan: 'Balcony overhang kicks in at row C, so views behind this may experience cut-off at the top of the stage.' Double-digit side seats (D24, G22) have partial sightlines. Fine for plays; poor for tall scenic musicals.

Rows B and C clear the Row A safety rail and preserve a steep but clean center view. Tripadvisor: 'Great view of the stage, although a bit of an angled view down.' Starting prices on SeatPlan as low as $68-$80. Steep rake is uncomfortable but preserves sightlines.

sg.n: Balcony Row A and Side L/R front rows
sg.ra: Row A front has a safety rail that cuts across the stage (SeatPlan, Playbill, Tripadvisor all independently confirm). TickPick: Balcony L and R first two rows have partial views due to railing. Shorter patrons especially affected.
